concepts.title: Inertia and Newton's First Law
concepts.definition: Bodies resist changes to their motion: an object at rest stays at rest and a moving object keeps its velocity unless a net external force intervenes. This inertia scales with mass -- a loaded truck is harder to start and to stop than a bicycle at the same speed.
concepts.key_idea: No net force means no change in velocity -- motion needs no cause, only changes in motion do.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph104.txt lines 40-160 (sections 4.2 Aristotle's fallacy, 4.3 law of inertia, 4.4 Newton's first law, Galileo's inclined plane argument)

solution_steps.explain: With zero net external force the velocity -- including the zero velocity of rest -- never changes.
Inertia is the body's reluctance to change that state, and mass measures how much inertia it owns.
Sudden braking drops the support under a passenger while the body keeps its motion, which is inertia made visible.

concepts.title: Momentum and Newton's Second Law
concepts.definition: Momentum, mass times velocity, is the quantity of motion a body carries. Newton's second law says the net external force equals the rate of change of momentum; for fixed mass this collapses to force equals mass times acceleration, the workhorse equation of mechanics.
concepts.key_idea: Force rewrites momentum per second -- push harder or longer and the momentum changes proportionally.

solution_steps.explain: Divide the velocity change by the time it takes to get the acceleration.
Mass times acceleration equals the net force doing the pushing.

concepts.title: Newton's Third Law and Conservation of Momentum
concepts.definition: Forces come in pairs: if body A pushes body B, B pushes A back equally hard along the same line. Because the pair acts and reacts inside the system, the total momentum of an isolated system never changes -- this conservation of momentum follows directly from the third law.
concepts.key_idea: Internal pushes shuffle momentum between bodies but never change the system total.

concepts.title: Friction: Static, Kinetic and Rolling
concepts.definition: Contact surfaces resist sliding through friction. Static friction adjusts itself up to a maximum set by the coefficient of static friction times the normal force; once sliding begins the smaller kinetic friction takes over, and rolling friction is smaller still. Friction is called a necessary evil -- it opposes motion yet enables walking and braking.
concepts.key_idea: Friction has a ceiling proportional to how hard the surfaces press -- exceed it and sliding starts.

concepts.title: Dynamics of Circular Motion
concepts.definition: Circular motion demands a centre-directed net force of size mass times speed squared over radius -- the centripetal force. Banked roads, curved tracks and a whirling stone on a string all supply this force in different guises; a vehicle's safe speed on a banked curve follows from resolving forces on the incline.
concepts.key_idea: Something must pull inward -- identify which real force plays centripetal in each situation.

solution_steps.explain: Mark every real force on the body: weight, normal, tension or friction.
The radial component of the real forces must equal m v squared over r.
For banked curves, resolving along and across the incline yields the friction-free ideal speed in terms of g, radius and banking angle.
